sections.title: Problem Formulation
sections.extract: A multi-agent system consists of a set of expert agents with different domain specializations. Let A = {a1, a2, ..., aN} denote the set of all available expert agents. In real systems, each expert agent is not hard- coded into the router through a fixed identifier; instead, it exposes its capabilities and responsibilities to the routing model through a natural-language description. sections.title: Dynamic Agent Addition
sections.extract: Traditional methods typically bind a router R to a fixed agent set A, when A changes R must be retrained. sections.extract: Selecting Multiple Agents. Traditional task routing typically formulates routing as a single-label classification problem:R(Prompt(q, A)) = ai ∈A meaning that each query can only be assigned to a sin- gle agent. sections.title: Training TCAR
sections.extract: To endow the router R with both multi-agent selection capabilities and interpretable reasoning, we adopt a two-stage[28] training strategy. We first apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT)[29] to teach the model the basic “reason–then–select” pattern. We then further enhance the quality of agent selection and the stability of reasoning through reward-based reinforcement learning using DAPO [30]. Supervised Fine-Tuning.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.extract: • Reasoning capability is a key factor for improving routing interpretability and robustness. • RL is an essential training stage that enhances recall while maintaining high precision. • The choice of RL initialization point is crucial; Slerp-based models offer stronger generalization and are less prone to entropy collapse during RL. 5
